results.claim: There is an explicit 76-shade implementation of the geometric controller below.
results.proof_sketch: A shade encodes a controller phase and role. Use disjoint blocks of sizes 6 for the two-robot line train, 18 for the radius-two and edge searches, 16 for row updates and handshakes, 14 for an ordinary slice change, 16 for the outer-corner reset, and 6 for stationary beacon/mode tags; the sum is 76. The search blocks encode only role, tested axis/sign, and a counter bounded by three. Each listed command is relational—toward/away from a colored neighbor or wall, or a specified stabilizer orbit. Hence it defines rules on local-view orbits. Give every unlisted view the idle, shade-preserving rule.

results.claim: The knight invariant supports an adversary-proof row scan and translation.
results.proof_sketch: For orthogonal unit directions a,r,f, write K(q;a,r,f) for travelers at q,q+a and a beacon at q+2r+f, with −a a wall direction. The travelers sweep the entire a-line and return. They then test both signs of one tangent axis to distance two; if the beacon is absent, they test the other axis. Thus they necessarily reach T=q+r,H=q+2r adjacent to B=q+2r+f. Now H enters B's old node while B moves ambiguously to q+r+f or q+3r+f. In the first branch T moves to q+r+a, B enters T's old node, and H moves to q+3r+f. In the second H first backs to q+r+f, then enters T's node while T moves inward. Both branches end in K(q+r;a,r,f).

results.claim: Every non-outer slice is completely scanned, and ordinary slice changes preserve a valid frame.
results.proof_sketch: Iterating the knight update scans rows until the beacon reaches the row wall. A wall signal then forms the penultimate-row pair; a finite two-axis search for the diagonal beacon forms the last-row pair, so every row is swept. At the last corner c, if c+f is not an outer-boundary node, put q=c+f. The ordinary transition first reaches q,c,c+2f. A robot chooses d∈{a,−r}; after another shift the positions are q,q+d,c+2f. The third robot chooses x∈{a,−r}. If x=e≠d, the result is D(q;d,e,f): pair q,q+d and beacon q+e+f. If x=d, contact is detected and the pair rotates, giving D(q;e,d,f). From D(q;a,r,f), the first row is swept and a four-round wall-signaled choreography establishes K(q+r;a,r,f).

results.claim: The outer-corner reset is safe for every symmetry choice.
results.proof_sketch: Let q=c+f be an outer corner, h=−f, and let the first ambiguous move select one edge direction d; let e be the other. It forms q,q+d,q+h. Sweep the h-line, re-form, and sweep the e-line. Then form q,q+d,q+2d. The front selects x∈{e,h} while the other two follow, giving s=q+d,s+d,s+d+x; let y be the other direction. Move the middle robot into the third's node and let the third move ±d. If it reaches s+2d+x, back the middle to s+x; otherwise advance the middle to s+2d+x and back the third to s+x. Finally rotate the robot at s+x into s while the robot at s moves to s+y. Every branch ends in K(s;y,d,x). Both possible row-zero y-lines were swept before this choice.

results.claim: Every execution perpetually explores every finite grid of side lengths at least four.
results.proof_sketch: A scan phase with frame (ℓ,r,f) covers every vertex except possibly the far f-face. At its reset corner let h=−f, choose d∈{ℓ,−r}, let e be the other edge direction, and choose the next floor x∈{h,e}. The reset sweeps both h- and e-lines. If x=h, the formerly omitted face is the next phase's first slice and is covered. If x=e, a vertex missed again must also lie on the far e-face. At the following reset, choosing floor −e covers it immediately; choosing floor h cannot omit it because its h-coordinate is at the near boundary; the sole remaining choice can omit it only when it lies on the reset's swept third-axis line. Hence every vertex is visited within at most three consecutive phases. All phases and searches terminate on finite grids, so every vertex is visited infinitely often.

final_writeup:
Theorem. Exactly three Batdroids with visibility one and no common chirality solve PEP ambiguously with at most 76 shades.

Choose an initial grid corner q and three inward orthogonal directions a,r,f. Put the Batdroids at q, q+a, and q+2r+f in suitable role shades. Include all symmetric images of these configurations in Init.

Two local invariants are used:

K(q;a,r,f) = {q,q+a,q+2r+f}, the knight invariant;
D(q;a,r,f) = {q,q+a,q+r+f}, the diagonal invariant.

Line engine. Two adjacent, differently shaded travelers move as a train: the front moves away from the rear and the rear enters the front's old node. At the opposite wall the front side-steps to any valid tangent node while the rear follows; next, the wall robot moves away from that wall while the side robot enters its old node. This reverses the train without collision or an edge swap. The analogous maneuver restores it at the starting wall. Thus every node of the line is visited.

Knight search and update. After sweeping the line of K(q), the pair tests tangent directions from q. It walks two steps in one sign, reverses using role shades, tests the opposite sign when valid, returns to q, and tests the other tangent axis. The bounded controller therefore reaches q+2r, the unique tested point adjacent to the beacon q+2r+f. The resulting positions are T=q+r, H=q+2r, B=q+2r+f.

H now enters B's old node and B's symmetric view permits B±r. If B moves to q+r+f, T moves inward to q+r+a, B enters T's old node, and H moves to q+3r+f. If B moves directly to q+3r+f, H backs to q+r+f and then enters T's old node while T moves inward. Both cases give K(q+r). The choices are distinguishable by adjacency, so the same local transition table implements the branch.

Rows and ordinary slice changes. Repeating this operation scans successive rows. When q+2r reaches the row wall, a one-round color signal replaces the usual update: the pair is formed on the penultimate row. After that row is swept, a bounded search for the diagonal beacon q+r+f tests both tangent axes. The beacon accepts only an approach through q+r; the row wall lets it distinguish this from the orthogonal approach. This forms and sweeps the last row.

At the last corner c the configuration is c,c+a,c+f. If c+f is not an outer floor, set q=c+f. A four-stage shift reaches q,q+d,c+2f, where d is either a or −r. Let e denote the other direction. The robot at c+2f ambiguously chooses d or e. Choosing e gives pair q,q+d and beacon q+e+f. Choosing d makes it adjacent to q+d; after that robot signals, q moves to q+e while q+d enters q. This gives pair q,q+e and beacon q+d+f. Thus either outcome is a valid D frame, possibly with line and row exchanged.

From D, sweep row zero. On return the row-origin wall identifies r, so the travelers rendezvous at q,q+r,q+r+f. A bounded signaled choreography moves the beacon either directly or by one corrective train step and ends in K(q+r). Hence all remaining rows are handled by the knight engine.

Outer reset. Suppose q=c+f is an outer corner and put h=−f. The first reset round forms q,q+d,q+h, where d is adversarially one of the two inward edge directions; call the other e. Sweep the full h-line with q+d stationary. Re-form the pair and sweep the full e-line with q+h stationary. Two train rounds then form q,q+d,q+2d.

The front chooses x∈{e,h}, while its two followers advance, producing T=s=q+d, H=s+d, B=s+d+x. Let y be the other member of {e,h}. H enters B's old node and B moves ±d. If B reaches s+2d+x, H backs to s+x. Otherwise H reaches s+2d+x while B follows, and B then backs to s+x. Finally the robot at s moves to s+y while the robot at s+x enters s. The result is K(s;y,d,x). Since the reset already swept both candidate y-lines at row zero, the new first slice is fully covered when the knight engine starts at row one.

Coverage. A phase with fixed floor direction f covers every vertex except possibly the far f-face. At reset, if the new floor is h=−f, that face is the new first slice. Otherwise the new floor is e and the new line is h. A vertex missed twice must lie on both far faces and agrees with the next reset corner in the h-coordinate. At the next reset, reversing e covers it; selecting h cannot omit it; selecting the remaining edge can omit it only if it lies on the full edge-line swept by the reset. Thus every vertex is visited within at most three phases, hence infinitely often.

Shade audit. Assign distinct role-state shades in blocks: 6 for the line train, 18 for the two bounded searches, 16 for row updates and handshakes, 14 for the ordinary slice transition including its contact signal, 16 for the outer reset, and 6 stationary beacon/mode shades. Total: 76. Every prescribed move is determined by colored neighbors and walls or is precisely one stabilizer orbit; unreachable views are assigned idle. All listed motions are exclusive. Therefore this is a valid ambiguous 76-shade algorithm solving PEP.
